arguments.heading: What happened at the argument
paragraphs: Ms. Lenz argued that no clearly established federal law was violated in this case.
Mr. Komp argued that prior precedent holds no basis to distinguish between guilt and penalty phases.
Justice Sotomayor questioned whether an affirmative instruction allowing the use of silence would be constitutional.
Justice Kagan asked if the Fifth Amendment has no role in sentencing hearings once a defendant is eligible for death.

sections.heading: What this case is about
paragraphs: This case tests the scope of the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination. The core conflict involves whether that protection extends to the sentencing phase of a capital trial. the side that brought the case argues the right applies fully. the opposing side argues the right does not bar such inferences at that stage.

sections.heading: What each side wants
paragraphs: the side that brought the case wants the Court to hold that the Fifth Amendment bars the jury from using the defendant's silence against him during sentencing.
the opposing side wants the Court to hold that the Fifth Amendment does not bar the jury from using the defendant's silence against him during sentencing.

sections.heading: What each side says
paragraphs: the side that brought the case argues that the Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination applies equally to the guilt and penalty phases of a capital trial.
the opposing side argues that the Fifth Amendment does not prohibit a jury from drawing inferences from a defendant's silence during a sentencing hearing.

sections.heading: What the justices asked
paragraphs: Justice Sotomayor asked whether the Fifth Amendment permits a judge to instruct a jury to use a defendant's silence against him.
Justice Scalia asked whether a judge could inform a jury that a defendant chose not to testify during a punishment hearing.

sections.heading: Why it matters
paragraphs: The outcome defines the practical limits of the right against self-incrimination. It determines whether defendants can remain silent during sentencing without facing adverse inferences. This affects the conduct of all capital sentencing proceedings nationwide.
